claim: Functional CRISPR-Cas systems are absent from multidrug-resistant (MDR) Enterococcus faecalis.
source: It was previously observed that functional CRISPR-Cas systems are absent from multidrug-resistant (MDR) Enterococcus faecalis, which only possess an orphan CRISPR locus, termed CRISPR2, lacking cas genes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript.

claim: MDR E. faecalis possess an orphan CRISPR locus termed CRISPR2 that lacks cas genes.
source: It was previously observed that functional CRISPR-Cas systems are absent from multidrug-resistant (MDR) Enterococcus faecalis, which only possess an orphan CRISPR locus, termed CRISPR2, lacking cas genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the genetic composition of MDR E. faecalis strains.

claim: CRISPR2 can be reactivated for genome defense in MDR strains.
source: We demonstrate that CRISPR2 can be reactivated for genome defense in MDR strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cas9-dependent decreases in conjugation frequencies when CRISPR2 is activated.

claim: E. faecalis transiently maintains CRISPR targets despite active CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: Interestingly, we observe that E. faecalis transiently maintains CRISPR targets despite active CRISPR-Cas systems.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing transconjugants can be obtained and maintained for days despite CRISPR targeting.

claim: When selection for the CRISPR target is present, toxic CRISPR spacers are lost over time.
source: Subsequently, if selection for the CRISPR target is present, toxic CRISPR spacers are lost over time, while in the absence of selection, CRISPR targets are lost over time.
evidence: This is supported by the spacer deletion assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of selection for the CRISPR target, CRISPR targets are lost over time.
source: Subsequently, if selection for the CRISPR target is present, toxic CRISPR spacers are lost over time, while in the absence of selection, CRISPR targets are lost over time.
evidence: This is supported by plasmid maintenance data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Forced maintenance of CRISPR targets induces a fitness cost in E. faecalis.
source: We find that forced maintenance of CRISPR targets induces a fitness cost that can be exploited to alter heterogeneous E. faecalis populations.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data showing extended lag phase in transconjugants with CRISPR-targeted plasmids.

claim: The fitness cost from forced maintenance of CRISPR targets can be exploited to alter heterogeneous E. faecalis populations.
source: We find that forced maintenance of CRISPR targets induces a fitness cost that can be exploited to alter heterogeneous E. faecalis populations.
evidence: This is supported by conjugation-competition assay data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 8.

claim: E. faecalis is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen that commensally inhabits the gastrointestinal tracts of humans and other mammals.
source: Enterococcus faecalis is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen that commensally inhabits the gastrointestinal tracts of humans and other mammals (Lebreton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about E. faecalis supported by citation.

claim: Enterococcal infections are considered serious public health threats.
source: Enterococcal infections are considered serious public health threats, and rising antibiotic resistance makes these infections particularly difficult to treat (Arias and Murray, 2012; Kristich et al., 2014; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2014; Sievert et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to public health and scientific literature.

claim: Rising antibiotic resistance makes enterococcal infections particularly difficult to treat.
source: Enterococcal infections are considered serious public health threats, and rising antibiotic resistance makes these infections particularly difficult to treat (Arias and Murray, 2012; Kristich et al., 2014; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2014; Sievert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to scientific and public health literature.

claim: MDR isolates of E. faecalis possess expanded genomes relative to more drug-sensitive isolates.
source: Sequence analysis of multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolates of E. faecalis reveals that they typically possess expanded genomes relative to more drug-sensitive isolates and have acquired large segments of mobile DNA in the form of prophage, genomic islands, transposons, and plasmids (Raven et al., 2016; Palmer et al., 2012; Paulsen et al., 2003; Bourgogne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic sequencing studies.

claim: MDR E. faecalis have acquired large segments of mobile DNA in the form of prophage, genomic islands, transposons, and plasmids.
source: Sequence analysis of multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolates of E. faecalis reveals that they typically possess expanded genomes relative to more drug-sensitive isolates and have acquired large segments of mobile DNA in the form of prophage, genomic islands, transposons, and plasmids (Raven et al., 2016; Palmer et al., 2012; Paulsen et al., 2003; Bourgogne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic sequencing studies.

claim: Mobile DNA elements in MDR E. faecalis often encode antibiotic resistance determinants and virulence factors.
source: These extraneous DNA elements often encode antibiotic resistance determinants and virulence factors that facilitate host infection and colonization, thus making the horizontal dissemination of DNA one of the prime causative factors for the emergence of MDR E. faecalis (Palmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Horizontal dissemination of DNA is one of the prime causative factors for the emergence of MDR E. faecalis.
source: These extraneous DNA elements often encode antibiotic resistance determinants and virulence factors that facilitate host infection and colonization, thus making the horizontal dissemination of DNA one of the prime causative factors for the emergence of MDR E. faecalis (Palmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CRISPR-Cas are adaptive immune systems employed by bacteria to reduce the prevalence of mobile genetic elements.
source: Clustered Regularly-Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats and their associated Cas proteins (CRISPR-Cas) are adaptive immune systems employed by bacteria to reduce the prevalence of mobile genetic elements (MGEs), such as bacteriophage and plasmids, in their populations (Rath et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CRISPR-Cas systems supported by citation.

claim: Some E. faecalis encode Type II CRISPR-Cas systems defined by the presence of cas9.
source: Some E. faecalis encode Type II CRISPR-Cas systems, defined by the presence of cas9, and which consist of two main components: a CRISPR array and cas genes.
evidence: This is supported by prior characterization studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Type II CRISPR-Cas systems consist of two main components: a CRISPR array and cas genes.
source: Some E. faecalis encode Type II CRISPR-Cas systems, defined by the presence of cas9, and which consist of two main components: a CRISPR array and cas genes.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Type II CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: The CRISPR array consists of 36 bp repetitive DNA elements (repeats) interspersed by 30 bp sequences usually derived from foreign DNA (spacers).
source: The CRISPR array consists of 36 bp repetitive DNA elements (repeats) interspersed by 30 bp sequences usually derived from foreign DNA (spacers).
evidence: This describes the structural organization of CRISPR arrays in E. faecalis.

claim: The cognate spacer sequence present in foreign DNA is termed the protospacer.
source: The cognate spacer sequence present in foreign DNA, termed the protospacer, is usually located proximally to a conserved DNA sequence referred to as the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
evidence: This is standard CRISPR terminology.

claim: The protospacer is usually located proximally to a conserved DNA sequence referred to as the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
source: The cognate spacer sequence present in foreign DNA, termed the protospacer, is usually located proximally to a conserved DNA sequence referred to as the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
evidence: This is a well-established feature of CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: During CRISPR interference, the Cas9 endonuclease is guided to DNA targets by CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs).
source: During CRISPR interference, the Cas9 endonuclease is guided to DNA targets by CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), which are processed transcripts derived from the CRISPR array.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Type II CRISPR-Cas systems, supported by citations.

claim: crRNAs are processed transcripts derived from the CRISPR array.
source: During CRISPR interference, the Cas9 endonuclease is guided to DNA targets by CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), which are processed transcripts derived from the CRISPR array.
evidence: This is a well-established aspect of CRISPR-Cas mechanism.

claim: An active Cas9-crRNA targeting complex is associated with a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA).
source: An active Cas9-crRNA targeting complex is also associated with a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA), which is partially complementary to the repeats of the CRISPR array.
evidence: This describes the composition of the Type II CRISPR-Cas targeting complex.

claim: tracrRNA is partially complementary to the repeats of the CRISPR array.
source: An active Cas9-crRNA targeting complex is also associated with a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA), which is partially complementary to the repeats of the CRISPR array.
evidence: This is a well-established feature of Type II CRISPR-Cas systems.

claim: The Cas9 targeting complex samples PAMs in DNA, and once it encounters a match to the affiliated crRNA spacer sequence, Cas9 creates a double-stranded break in the target DNA.
source: This targeting complex samples PAMs in DNA, and once it encounters a match to the affiliated crRNA spacer sequence, Cas9 creates a double-stranded break in the target DNA.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of CRISPR interference.

claim: Three Type II CRISPR occur with variable distributions in the E. faecalis species.
source: Three Type II CRISPR occur with variable distributions in the E. faecalis species, including two that possess cas genes (CRISPR1 and CRISPR3, which are Type II-A systems [Fonfara et al., 2014]), and one orphan array (CRISPR2) that is ubiquitous but lacks associated cas genes (Bourgogne et al., 2008; Palmer and Gilmore, 2010; Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: CRISPR1 and CRISPR3 possess cas genes and are Type II-A systems.
source: Three Type II CRISPR occur with variable distributions in the E. faecalis species, including two that possess cas genes (CRISPR1 and CRISPR3, which are Type II-A systems [Fonfara et al., 2014]), and one orphan array (CRISPR2) that is ubiquitous but lacks associated cas genes (Bourgogne et al., 2008; Palmer and Gilmore, 2010; Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CRISPR2 is ubiquitous in E. faecalis but lacks associated cas genes.
source: Three Type II CRISPR occur with variable distributions in the E. faecalis species, including two that possess cas genes (CRISPR1 and CRISPR3, which are Type II-A systems [Fonfara et al., 2014]), and one orphan array (CRISPR2) that is ubiquitous but lacks associated cas genes (Bourgogne et al., 2008; Palmer and Gilmore, 2010; Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: The orphan CRISPR2 locus possesses repeats identical to those in CRISPR1, but not CRISPR3.
source: The orphan locus possesses repeats identical to those in CRISPR1, but not CRISPR3.
evidence: This is a sequence comparison observation.

claim: The consensus PAM sequences for CRISPR1-Cas and CRISPR2 are identical (NGG).
source: Further, the consensus PAM sequences for CRISPR1-Cas and CRISPR are identical (NGG), while the PAM for CRISPR3 is distinct (NNRTA) (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The PAM for CRISPR3 is distinct (NNRTA).
source: Further, the consensus PAM sequences for CRISPR1-Cas and CRISPR are identical (NGG), while the PAM for CRISPR3 is distinct (NNRTA) (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The cas9 associated with CRISPR3 is distinct in sequence and function from the CRISPR1 cas9.
source: The cas9 associated with CRISPR3 is distinct in sequence and function from the CRISPR1 cas9.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and functional studies.

claim: CRISPR3-Cas9 cannot confer defense from conjugative plasmids using CRISPR2 spacers.
source: We have previously shown that CRISPR3-Cas9 cannot confer defense from conjugative plasmids using CRISPR2 spacers (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: An inverse correlation exists between the occurrence of Type II CRISPR-Cas systems and antibiotic resistance in E. faecalis.
source: An inverse correlation between the occurrence of Type II CRISPR-Cas systems and antibiotic resistance has been reported for E. faecalis (Palmer and Gilmore, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior observational study.

claim: All E. faecalis isolates possess a CRISPR2.
source: All E. faecalis isolates possess a CRISPR2, but most MDR strains lack the functional CRISPR1-Cas or CRISPR3-Cas systems (Palmer and Gilmore, 2010; Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: Most MDR E. faecalis strains lack the functional CRISPR1-Cas or CRISPR3-Cas systems.
source: All E. faecalis isolates possess a CRISPR2, but most MDR strains lack the functional CRISPR1-Cas or CRISPR3-Cas systems (Palmer and Gilmore, 2010; Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: V583 is a model MDR E. faecalis strain and was the first fully sequenced vancomycin-resistant isolate in the U.S.
source: V583 is a model MDR E. faecalis strain, and was the first fully sequenced vancomycin-resistant isolate in the U.S. (Paulsen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original sequencing study.

claim: V583 possesses an expanded genome relative to commensal isolates.
source: It possesses an expanded genome relative to commensal isolates, and its sole CRISPR locus is the orphan CRISPR2 (Palmer et al., 2012; Bourgogne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic analysis studies.

claim: V583's sole CRISPR locus is the orphan CRISPR2.
source: It possesses an expanded genome relative to commensal isolates, and its sole CRISPR locus is the orphan CRISPR2 (Palmer et al., 2012; Bourgogne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic analysis studies.

claim: CRISPR-Cas lowers the frequency of acquisition of large (50–70 kbp) conjugative pheromone responsive plasmids (PRPs) in E. faecalis T11.
source: We have previously reported that CRISPR-Cas lowers the frequency of acquisition of large (50–70 kbp) conjugative pheromone responsive plasmids (PRPs) in E. faecalis T11, a strain closely related to V583 but lacking the HGT-driven genome expansion characteristic of V583 (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: E. faecalis T11 is closely related to V583 but lacks the HGT-driven genome expansion characteristic of V583.
source: We have previously reported that CRISPR-Cas lowers the frequency of acquisition of large (50–70 kbp) conjugative pheromone responsive plasmids (PRPs) in E. faecalis T11, a strain closely related to V583 but lacking the HGT-driven genome expansion characteristic of V583 (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CK111SSp(pCF10-101) is an effective donor that can mobilize pKH-derivatives into a variety of E. faecalis strains.
source: CK111SSp(pCF10-101) (Kristich et al., 2007) was found to be an effective donor that was able to mobilize pKH-derivatives into a variety of strains.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: E. faecalis Merz96 and DS5 both showed bactericidal activity against CK111SSp(pCF10-101).
source: However, E. faecalis Merz96 and DS5 both showed bactericidal activity against CK111SSp(pCF10-101). Zones of inhibition were observed after spotting overnight cultures of Merz96 and DS5 onto CK111SSp(pCF10-101) lawns (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 are the most prevalent CRISPR loci in E. faecalis.
source: CRISPR1-cas and CRISPR2 are the most prevalent CRISPR loci in E. faecalis (Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior characterization study.

claim: CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 arrays contain identical repeats and differ only in their conserved locations in the chromosome and in the sequence of the terminal repeat.
source: These CRISPR arrays contain identical repeats and differ only in their conserved locations in the chromosome and in the sequence of the terminal repeat (discussed later).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: ATCC 4200RF was isolated from the bloodstream of a rheumatic fever patient in 1926, two years prior to the discovery of penicillin.
source: We first assessed ATCC 4200RF, isolated from the bloodstream of a rheumatic fever patient in 1926, two years prior to the discovery of penicillin (Birkhaug and Schilling, 1927).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original isolation report.

claim: pKHS244 had a 56-fold lower acquisition rate than pKH12 in ATCC 4200RF.
source: We found that pKHS244 had a 56-fold lower acquisition rate than pKH12, and this phenotype was lost in ATCC 4200RFΔcas9, confirming that the reduction in conjugation frequency was due to CRISPR interference (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The reduction in conjugation frequency of pKHS244 in ATCC 4200RF is due to CRISPR interference.
source: We found that pKHS244 had a 56-fold lower acquisition rate than pKH12, and this phenotype was lost in ATCC 4200RFΔcas9, confirming that the reduction in conjugation frequency was due to CRISPR interference (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is confirmed by the loss of phenotype in the cas9 deletion mutant.

claim: OG1RF is an oral commensal isolate that has been well characterized.
source: OG1RF is an oral commensal isolate that has been well characterized (Dunny et al., 1978; Bourgogne et al., 2008; Gold et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: DS5 is an erythromycin and tetracycline resistant isolate first described in 1974.
source: DS5 is an erythromycin and tetracycline resistant isolate first described in 1974, and contains three extrachromosomal plasmids (Clewell et al., 1974) despite the fact that it possesses the entire CRISPR1-Cas system (Palmer and Gilmore, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: DS5 contains three extrachromosomal plasmids despite possessing the entire CRISPR1-Cas system.
source: DS5 is an erythromycin and tetracycline resistant isolate first described in 1974, and contains three extrachromosomal plasmids (Clewell et al., 1974) despite the fact that it possesses the entire CRISPR1-Cas system (Palmer and Gilmore, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 are functionally linked in E. faecalis T11.
source: We have previously established that CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 are functionally linked in E. faecalis T11 (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: A cas9-dependent decrease in conjugation frequency of pKHS11 relative to pKH12 was observed in ATCC 4200RF.
source: We confirmed this in ATCC 4200RF with plasmid pKHS11, which is targeted by S11 on the ATCC 4200RF CRISPR2 locus. We observed a cas9-dependent decrease in conjugation frequency of pKHS11 relative to pKH12 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: V583 and Merz96 are both MDR bloodstream infection isolates.
source: We then sought to examine if interaction between CRISPR1 Cas9 and CRISPR2 was preserved in MDR strains that natively lacked the CRISPR1-Cas system, since that had yet to be determined. We used the hospital-adapted strains V583 and Merz96, both MDR bloodstream infection isolates (Sahm et al., 1989; Harrington et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior reports.

claim: Cas9-dependent decreases in conjugation frequencies of protospacer-bearing pKHSX plasmids relative to pKH12 were observed for both V583 and Merz96 derivatives.
source: We observed cas9-dependent decreases in conjugation frequencies of protospacer-bearing pKHSX plasmids relative to pKH12 for both V583 and Merz96 derivatives (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Bidirectional transcripts spanning the CRISPR2 region in V583 have been identified by previous transcriptional profiling.
source: Previous transcriptional profiling performed in E. faecalis V583 (Fouquier d'Hérouel et al., 2011; Innocenti et al., 2015) identified bidirectional transcripts spanning the CRISPR2 region in V583.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior transcriptional profiling studies.

claim: The transcriptional start site for the CRISPR2 transcript occurs at 85 bp upstream of the first nucleotide of the first CRISPR2 repeat.
source: The transcriptional start site we identified for the CRISPR2 transcript occurs at 85 bp upstream of the first nucleotide of the first CRISPR2 repeat, which agrees with previous findings (Innocenti et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on primer extension data and agrees with prior findings.

claim: CRISPR2 transcription is required for genome defense.
source: To determine if CRISPR2 transcription is required for genome defense, ~50 bp of its promoter was deleted from V649, creating the strain V254. V254 shows conjugation frequencies for pKHS67 similar to that of pKH12 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing loss of defense when the promoter is deleted.

claim: Functional linkage of CRISPR2 and CRISPR1-Cas9 is preserved across diverse lineages of E. faecalis.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that functional linkage of CRISPR2 and CRISPR1-Cas9 is preserved across diverse lineages of E. faecalis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing CRISPR defense across multiple strains.

claim: CRISPR2 can be activated for genome defense in cas deficient MDR strains of E. faecalis.
source: Moreover, CRISPR2 can be activated for genome defense in cas deficient MDR strains of E. faecalis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing CRISPR defense in V583 and Merz96 derivatives with introduced cas9.

claim: In many CRISPR-Cas loci, the terminal CRISPR repeat is degenerated in sequence relative to the direct repeats.
source: In many CRISPR-Cas loci, the terminal CRISPR repeat is degenerated in sequence relative to the direct repeats (Touchon and Rocha, 2010; Horvath et al., 2008; Almendros et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CRISPR2 terminal repeats completely degenerate after 19 bp.
source: CRISPR2 terminal repeats completely degenerate after 19 bp, and the majority of arrays (including in V583) contain two polymorphisms within those 19 bp.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of CRISPR1 terminal repeats degenerate after 22 bp.
source: These two polymorphisms are not observed in the majority of CRISPR1 terminal repeats, which degenerate after 22 bp (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The degeneracy of the terminal repeats of both CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 causes a loss of function in the terminal spacer.
source: We hypothesized that the degeneracy of the terminal repeats of both CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 causes a loss of function in the terminal spacer, since the association of the crRNA with the tracrRNA would be disrupted.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: pKHSL conjugation frequency was equivalent to pKH12 in V649, revealing the lack of function of S12.
source: As predicted, pKHSL conjugation frequency was equivalent to pKH12 in V649, revealing the lack of function of S12.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Terminal spacers in both the CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 arrays in ATCC 4200RF are non-functional.
source: This phenomenon was also apparent for terminal spacers in both the CRISPR1 and CRISPR2 arrays in ATCC 4200RF, as the deletion of cas9 had no effect on the conjugation frequencies of plasmids bearing a terminal protospacer (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Replacing the terminal repeat with a direct repeat activates S12 for interference in V485.
source: To confirm that this was due to the degenerated repeat, we replaced the terminal repeat in V649 with a direct repeat, creating the strain V485 (Figure 2a). In V485, S12 is active for interference (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Transconjugants with CRISPR-targeted plasmids can be obtained at approximately ~10^5 CFU/mL despite intact CRISPR-Cas interference machinery in V649.
source: Despite the fact that the intact CRISPR-Cas interference machinery in V649 targets pKHS67 for cleavage, we were still able to obtain transconjugants at approximately ~105 CFU/mL, in agreement with previous findings for the native CRISPR3-Cas system of E. faecalis T11 (Price et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: Cas9-dependent plasmid loss was observed in pKHS67 transconjugants in the absence of selection for the plasmid.
source: Cas9-dependent plasmid loss was observed in pKHS67 transconjugants in the absence of selection for the plasmid (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CRISPR adaptation (i.e., new spacer addition) against pKHS67 was not observed.
source: CRISPR adaptation (i.e., new spacer addition) against pKHS67 was not observed.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations during passaging experiments.

claim: The CRISPR-Cas machinery was functional in the V649 transconjugants prior to conjugation.
source: We infer that the CRISPR-Cas machinery was functional in the V649 transconjugants prior to conjugation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of cas9-dependent plasmid loss over time.

claim: Spacer loss events occurred in 2 of 4 V649 pKHS67 transconjugants passaged with antibiotic selection for the plasmid.
source: Amplification of CRISPR2 from each passage revealed spacer loss events in 2 of 4 V649 pKHS67 transconjugants passaged with antibiotic selection for the plasmid (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Two V649 pKHS67 transconjugants maintained pKHS67 with selection over the course of 14 days with no detectable spacer deletion events.
source: The other 2 V649 pKHS67 transconjugants maintained pKHS67 with selection over the course of 14 days with no detectable spacer deletion events.
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data.

claim: E. faecalis cells can proliferate for days with their CRISPR-Cas system in conflict with a CRISPR target.
source: Importantly, we observe that E. faecalis cells can proliferate for days with their CRISPR-Cas system in conflict with a CRISPR target.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the passaging experiments showing transconjugants can be maintained for 14 days.

claim: Forced maintenance of a CRISPR target results in a fitness cost to the E. faecalis cell.
source: In E. faecalis, forced maintenance of a CRISPR target results in a fitness cost to the cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth curve data showing extended lag phase.

claim: When selection for the plasmid is present, the most competitive mutants have compromised the integrity of the CRISPR-Cas machinery likely through multiple mechanisms, one of which is spacer deletion.
source: When selection for the plasmid is present, the most competitive mutants have compromised the integrity of the CRISPR-Cas machinery likely through multiple mechanisms, one of which is spacer deletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of spacer deletions in some passaged transconjugants.

claim: In the absence of selection, the fitness cost is overcome by plasmid loss.
source: In the absence of selection, the fitness cost is overcome by plasmid loss.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the plasmid maintenance data in Figure 3.

claim: Terminal spacers are the least likely to be lost from the CRISPR array.
source: Therefore, terminal spacers are the least likely to be lost from the CRISPR array.
evidence: This is based on the conservation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Terminal spacers correspond to the 'oldest' memories of the CRISPR array, since adaptation occurs at the leader end.
source: Moreover, it is widely understood that terminal spacers correspond to the 'oldest' memories of the CRISPR array, since adaptation occurs at the leader end (Barrangou et al., 2007; Sternberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on CRISPR adaptation.

claim: Only non-terminal spacer deletions were observed when selection was applied to V649 pKHS67 transconjugants.
source: In our spacer deletion assay, we observed only non-terminal spacer deletions when selection was applied to V649 pKHS67 transconjugants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Terminal and non-terminal spacer deletions were observed in 2 of 3 V485 pKHS67 transconjugants passaged for 14 days.
source: We also passaged V485 pKHS67 transconjugants for 14 days, observing terminal and non-terminal spacer deletions in 2 of 3 cases.
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data.

claim: Three terminal spacer deletion events were observed in V485, while no terminal spacer deletion events were observed in V649.
source: Three terminal spacer deletion events were observed in V485, while no terminal spacer deletion events were observed in V649 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is directly observed experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Terminal degenerate repeats in CRISPR2 prevent terminal spacer deletion and facilitate the persistence of the ubiquitous CRISPR2 array in E. faecalis.
source: This observation provides evidence that terminal degenerate repeats in CRISPR2 prevent terminal spacer deletion and facilitate the persistence of the ubiquitous CRISPR2 array in E. faecalis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential spacer deletion patterns.

claim: Transconjugants with plasmids in conflict with CRISPR spacers exhibited an extended lag phase when grown with selection (chloramphenicol).
source: We observed that transconjugants with plasmids in conflict with CRISPR spacers exhibited an extended lag phase when grown with selection (chloramphenicol), while control transconjugants exhibited no such defect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: When pKHS67 is conjugated to V649, the V649 CFU is dramatically reduced in the population when passaged in chloramphenicol, while CK111SSp(pCF10-101) remains abundant.
source: However, when pKHS67 is conjugated to V649, the V649 CFU is dramatically reduced in the population when passaged in chloramphenicol, while CK111SSp(pCF10-101) remains abundant (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: V583 and V649 naturally outcompete CK111SSp(pCF10-101) in BHI when no CRISPR conflict is present.
source: Importantly, our data suggest that V583 and V649 naturally outcompete CK111SSp(pCF10-101) in BHI when no CRISPR conflict is present.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition assay data in Figure 5.

claim: When CRISPR conflict is applied, V649 is outcompeted by CK111SSp(pCF10-101).
source: However, when CRISPR conflict is applied, the opposite effect is seen.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the competition assay data in Figure 5.

claim: Competitive environments and CRISPR incompatibility can be used to remove certain MDR E. faecalis from a population in vitro.
source: This demonstrates that competitive environments and CRISPR incompatibility can be used to remove certain MDR E. faecalis from a population in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the competition assay data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: When pKHS67 is propagated in a mixed population, V649 falls to 0.001% of the population after chloramphenicol passage.
source: As expected, when pKHS67 is propagated in the population, V649 falls to 0.001% of the population after the chloramphenicol passage.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: When pKHS11 is propagated, ATCC 4200RF falls below the threshold of detection, and V649 and CK111SSp(pCF10-101) dominate the population.
source: However, when pKHS11 is propagated, ATCC 4200RF falls below the threshold of detection, and V649 and CK111SSp(pCF10-101) dominate the population.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: V583 is never removed from the population since it lacks a functional CRISPR-Cas system.
source: Expectedly, V583 is never removed from the population since it lacks a functional CRISPR-Cas system.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the competition assay data in Figure 6.

claim: PRPs are large mobilizable plasmids unique to the E. faecalis species that often encode toxin-antitoxin systems or bacteriocins to promote self-preservation.
source: In natural E. faecalis populations, antibiotic resistance genes and virulence factors are often disseminated on PRPs, which are large mobilizable plasmids unique to the E. faecalis species, and which often encode toxin-antitoxin systems or bacteriocins to promote self-preservation (Hirt et al., 2005; Weaver, 2012; Wardal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior characterization studies.

claim: CRISPR systems and their targets cannot coexist in the same cell in E. coli, Sulfolobus, and various streptococci.
source: It has been previously shown that CRISPR-Cas systems and their targets cannot coexist in the same cell. This phenomenon has been observed in E. coli, Sulfolobus, and various streptococci (Jiang et al., 2013a; Gudbergsdottir et al., 2011; Bikard et al., 2012; Marraffini and Sontheimer, 2010; Selle and Barrangou, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in other organisms.

claim: In S. epidermidis, transconjugants with CRISPR targets were detected at very low frequencies and all contained mutations that inactivated the CRISPR system.
source: In a thorough investigation of CRISPR-Cas in S. epidermidis, Jiang, et al detected transconjugants at very low frequencies, and found that they all contained mutations that inactivated the CRISPR system (Jiang et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CRISPR self-targeting induced growth inhibition and cellular elongation and filamentation in Pectobacterium atrosepticum.
source: Similarly, a dramatic inhibition of growth was observed when CRISPR self-targeting was induced in Pectobacterium atrosepticum, which led to growth inhibition and cellular elongation and filamentation, which are indicators of the SOS response (Vercoe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CRISPR-induced toxicity induces the SOS response in E. coli at low cas9 expression levels.
source: CRISPR-induced toxicity was also found to induce the SOS response in E. coli at low cas9 expression levels (Cui and Bikard, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CRISPR conflict does not result in recA up-regulation in E. faecalis.
source: This is in direct contrast to our findings, where CRISPR conflict does not result in recA up-regulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa displays characteristics of CRISPR interference similar to that of E. faecalis, where a targeted plasmid is acquired but gradually lost from the population over time.
source: However, Pseudomonas aeruginosa displays characteristics of CRISPR interference similar to that of E. faecalis, where a targeted plasmid is acquired, but gradually lost from the population over time due to CRISPR interference (Høyland-Kroghsbo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A cas9-dependent reduction in pCR2-ermB and pCR2-Phage1 conjugation frequency relative to pCR2 was observed.
source: Similar to native CRISPR-Cas defense, we observed a cas9-dependent reduction in pCR2-ermB and pCR2-Phage1 conjugation frequency relative to pCR2 (Figure 7a–b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7a-b.

claim: Targeting a native PRP in V649 was as detrimental to V649 as targeting a chromosomal region.
source: Nonetheless, our data show that targeting a native PRP in V649 was as detrimental to V649 as targeting a chromosomal region.
evidence: This is inferred from the conjugation frequency data in Figure 7.

claim: pTEF1 loss activates toxin-mediated killing via its predicted toxin-antitoxin system.
source: This is presumably because pTEF1 loss activates toxin-mediated killing via its predicted toxin-antitoxin system (Weaver, 2012).
evidence: This is inferred based on prior characterization of pTEF1 and supported by citation.

claim: V649 transconjugants containing pCR2-ermB retained phenotypic resistance to erythromycin despite CRISPR targeting of ermB.
source: Importantly, V649 transconjugants containing pCR2-ermB retained phenotypic resistance to erythromycin despite CRISPR targeting of ermB (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: V649 transconjugants containing pCR2-ermB exhibited a growth defect with chloramphenicol selection.
source: However, they exhibited a growth defect with chloramphenicol selection for pCR2-ermB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth curve data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of transconjugants that retained erythromycin resistance was reduced 261-fold when pCR2-ermB was conjugated into T11CR1.
source: However, the number of transconjugants that retained erythromycin resistance was reduced 261-fold when pCR2-ermB was conjugated into T11CR1 (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: pTEF1 loss is not well tolerated by V649 but pAM771 loss is easily tolerated by T11CR1.
source: We conclude that pTEF1 loss is not well tolerated by V649 but pAM771 loss is easily tolerated by T11CR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of ermB targeting in the two strains.

claim: When pCR2-ermB is propagated, erythromycin-resistant CFU decrease to 0.016% of the population.
source: When pCR2-ermB is propagated, erythromycin-resistant CFU decrease to 0.016% of the population, while the total V649 CFU falls below the threshold of detection after one passage in chloramphenicol.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Total V649 CFU falls below the threshold of detection after one passage in chloramphenicol when pCR2-ermB is propagated.
source: When pCR2-ermB is propagated, erythromycin-resistant CFU decrease to 0.016% of the population, while the total V649 CFU falls below the threshold of detection after one passage in chloramphenicol.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: pAM771, but not T11CR1, is suppressed by targeting ermB since loss of pAM771 is tolerated.
source: Taken together, we conclude that pAM771, but not T11CR1, is suppressed by targeting ermB since loss of pAM771 is tolerated, while V649 is eliminated if pCR2-ermB is propagated since loss of pTEF1 is not tolerated.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition assay data in Figure 8.

claim: V649 is eliminated if pCR2-ermB is propagated since loss of pTEF1 is not tolerated.
source: Taken together, we conclude that pAM771, but not T11CR1, is suppressed by targeting ermB since loss of pAM771 is tolerated, while V649 is eliminated if pCR2-ermB is propagated since loss of pTEF1 is not tolerated.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition assay data in Figure 8.

claim: CRISPR delivery via conjugation induces a fitness cost in the presence of selection that can be exploited in competitive environments to reduce the prevalence of specific genes and specific MDR strains from E. faecalis populations.
source: Our data indicate that CRISPR delivery via conjugation induces a fitness cost in the presence of selection that can be exploited in competitive environments to reduce the prevalence of specific genes and specific MDR strains from E. faecalis populations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the competition assay data throughout the Results section.

claim: Expression of chromosomal CRISPR targeting in E. coli induced the SOS response, specifically activating recA.
source: A previous study showed that expression of chromosomal CRISPR targeting in E. coli induced the SOS response, specifically activating recA (Cui and Bikard, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A 26-fold increase in recA transcript levels was observed in E. faecalis cultures treated with levofloxacin.
source: We observed a 26-fold increase in recA transcript levels in cultures treated with LVX, while V649 pCR2-Phage1 transconjugants displayed a 1.7-fold decrease in recA transcript levels relative to V649 pCR2 transconjugants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: V649 pCR2-Phage1 transconjugants displayed a 1.7-fold decrease in recA transcript levels relative to V649 pCR2 transconjugants.
source: We observed a 26-fold increase in recA transcript levels in cultures treated with LVX, while V649 pCR2-Phage1 transconjugants displayed a 1.7-fold decrease in recA transcript levels relative to V649 pCR2 transconjugants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A small but statistically significant increase in cell death was observed upon chromosomal CRISPR targeting.
source: We simultaneously performed live/dead assays and found a small but statistically significant increase in cell death upon chromosomal CRISPR targeting (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CRISPR chromosomal targeting does not induce a canonical DNA damage response in E. faecalis.
source: These results suggest that CRISPR chromosomal targeting does not induce a canonical DNA damage response in E. faecalis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of recA up-regulation upon CRISPR targeting.

claim: Terminal degenerate repeats and highly conserved terminal spacers are a common characteristic of many CRISPR systems.
source: Terminal degenerate repeats and highly conserved terminal spacers are a common characteristic of many CRISPR systems.
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: CRISPR2 terminal repeats can prevent terminal spacer deletion.
source: We provide evidence that CRISPR2 terminal repeats can prevent terminal spacer deletion, but the evolutionary advantage remains unclear, especially since it has been shown that a single direct repeat alone is sufficient to promote spacer adaptation in E. coli and S. thermophilus (Yosef et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spacer deletion assay data in Figure 4.

claim: A single direct repeat alone is sufficient to promote spacer adaptation in E. coli and S. thermophilus.
source: We provide evidence that CRISPR2 terminal repeats can prevent terminal spacer deletion, but the evolutionary advantage remains unclear, especially since it has been shown that a single direct repeat alone is sufficient to promote spacer adaptation in E. coli and S. thermophilus (Yosef et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The smallest CRISPR2 array observed in E. faecalis consists of a direct repeat followed by a single spacer and a terminal repeat.
source: In agreement with our findings, the smallest CRISPR2 array observed in E. faecalis consists of a direct repeat followed by a single spacer and a terminal repeat (Hullahalli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior characterization study.

claim: Degeneracy in the terminal repeat may have been selected over time, preventing complete loss of the CRISPR array.
source: Degeneracy in the terminal repeat may have been selected over time, preventing complete loss of the CRISPR array, and as a consequence, the terminal spacer lost CRISPR interference functionality.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Terminal spacers are functionally inactive for genome defense and are not subject to conflicts with protospacer-bearing elements, which may explain their conservation.
source: Moreover, that terminal spacers are functionally inactive for genome defense means that they are not subject to conflicts with protospacer-bearing elements, which may also explain their conservation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing terminal spacers are non-functional.

claim: The ability of targeted DNA to temporarily coexist with the CRISPR-Cas system is a particularly striking feature of CRISPR systems in E. faecalis.
source: A particularly striking feature of CRISPR systems in E. faecalis is the ability of the targeted DNA to temporarily coexist with the CRISPR-Cas system.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing transient maintenance of CRISPR targets.

claim: The delayed activity of CRISPR in P. aeruginosa was attributed to the ability for plasmid replication to titrate out Cas9 targeting complexes.
source: Similar to our observations in E. faecalis, strikingly large numbers of 'escape mutants' were observed for P. aeruginosa. This delayed activity was attributed to the ability for plasmid replication to titrate out Cas9 targeting complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on P. aeruginosa.

claim: Plasmid copy number titrating Cas9 targeting complexes does not completely explain the transient tolerance of CRISPR targets in E. faecalis.
source: Our study is distinct in that we include chromosome-targeting constructs, which would not be limited by plasmid replication, and find that similarly large transconjugant pools appear. This suggests that plasmid copy number titrating Cas9 targeting complexes does not completely explain the transient tolerance of CRISPR targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing large transconjugant pools even with chromosomal targeting.

claim: The transconjugants with CRISPR targets may be better classified as 'unstable' rather than 'escape mutants'.
source: Our data suggest that these transconjugants may better be classified as 'unstable'.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transconjugants eventually lose either the plasmid or the spacer depending on selection.

claim: The basis for transient tolerance of CRISPR targets may be efficient DNA repair or stress response mechanisms that allow cells to survive chromosome cleavage by Cas9.
source: The basis for these transconjugants may be efficient DNA repair or stress response mechanisms that allow cells to survive chromosome cleavage by Cas9, or the induction of genes that transiently repress the CRISPR system, but this is speculative.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Low native expression of cas9 could explain the transient tolerance phenotype.
source: It is also possible that this phenotype is due to low native expression of cas9.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about a potential mechanism.

claim: E. faecalis may have evolved to temporarily tolerate CRISPR targets as a mechanism to enhance population-level genetic diversity.
source: If this were the case, it would suggest that E. faecalis has evolved to temporarily tolerate CRISPR targets, perhaps as a mechanism to enhance population-level genetic diversity. This could prove beneficial, particularly in environments where acquisition of a mobile genetic element is advantageous for survival.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary implications.

claim: CRISPR targeting to distinguish very closely related strains was first demonstrated in E. coli.
source: CRISPR targeting to distinguish very closely related strains was first demonstrated in E. coli (Gomaa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Delivery of CRISPR-Cas systems is a major challenge to establishing CRISPR therapeutics.
source: Delivery of CRISPR-Cas systems is a major challenge to establishing CRISPR therapeutics, and has been studied using bacteriophage (Citorik et al., 2014; Bikard et al., 2014; Yosef et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on CRISPR delivery.

claim: A major limitation to phage delivery of CRISPR systems is narrow host range and incomplete delivery.
source: However, a major limitation to phage delivery of CRISPR systems is narrow host range and incomplete delivery (Beisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: E. faecalis readily acquires resistance to phage via receptor mutations.
source: Moreover, E. faecalis has been shown to readily acquire resistance to phage via receptor mutations (Duerkop et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Conjugative delivery of CRISPR systems has been previously examined in E. coli.
source: Conjugative delivery has been previously examined in E. coli (Citorik et al., 2014), but the investigators found very few viable transconjugants when introducing plasmids targeting the host chromosome via CRISPR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In E. coli, very few viable transconjugants were found when introducing plasmids targeting the host chromosome via CRISPR.
source: Conjugative delivery has been previously examined in E. coli (Citorik et al., 2014), but the investigators found very few viable transconjugants when introducing plasmids targeting the host chromosome via CRISPR.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A large pool of transconjugants readily emerges in E. faecalis despite CRISPR-Cas activity.
source: This is in contrast to what we observe in E. faecalis, where a large pool of transconjugants readily emerges despite CRISPR-Cas activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data throughout the Results section.

claim: CRISPR-Cas may be a viable tool to alter in vivo E. faecalis populations.
source: CRISPR-Cas may be a viable tool to alter in vivo E. faecalis populations as well.
evidence: This is speculative based on the in vitro results.

claim: PRPs have previously been shown to provide selective advantages in vivo through bacteriocin production.
source: PRPs have previously been shown to provide selective advantages in vivo through bacteriocin production, mimicking the antibiotic selection used in this study (Kommineni et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The use of CRISPR-Cas as a tool to modify population structure is extremely attractive due to its highly specific activity against particular strains, leaving the remainder of the microbiome intact.
source: The use of CRISPR-Cas a tool to modify population structure is extremely attractive, due to its highly specific activity against particular strains, leaving the remainder of the microbiome intact.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: CRISPR-Cas employed on conjugative vectors that target antibiotic resistance genes can actively suppress proliferation of other conjugative vectors that harbor the targeted genes.
source: As demonstrated by our in vitro work, CRISPR-Cas employed on conjugative vectors that target antibiotic resistance genes can actively suppress proliferation of other conjugative vectors that harbor the targeted genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Drug-sensitive E. faecalis are already used as commercial probiotics.
source: Furthermore, drug-sensitive E. faecalis are already used as commercial probiotics (Neuhaus et al., 2017; Domann et al., 2007; Fritzenwanker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The use of CRISPR targeting constructs in combination with cas9 to influence enterococcal populations could be helpful in reducing MDR enterococcal bloodstream infections in patients colonized with these organisms.
source: The use of CRISPR targeting constructs in combination with cas9 to influence enterococcal populations, perhaps using probiotic E. faecalis armed with narrow host range conjugative delivery vectors, could be helpful in reducing MDR enterococcal bloodstream infections in patients colonized with these organisms (Al-Nassir et al., 2008; Ubeda et al., 2010; Clutter et al., 2013; Rice, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications supported by citations to clinical studies.
